"'''Roses Are Red (My Love)'''" is a [[popular song]] composed by Al Byron and [[Paul Evans (musician)|Paul Evans]]. It was recorded by [[Bobby Vinton]], backed by Robert Mersey and his Orchestra, in New York City in February 1962, and released in April 1962, and the song was his first hit.<ref name="BillboardHot100"/><ref name="ReferenceA">"Bobby Vinton's All-Time Greatest Hits," Varese (Vintage) Sarabande CD compilation, copyright 2003</ref>

"Roses Are Red (My Love)" is a popular song composed by Al Byron and Paul Evans. It was recorded by Bobby Vinton, backed by Robert Mersey and his Orchestra, in New York City in February 1962, and released in April 1962, and the song was his first hit.

sections.heading: Bobby Vinton version
sections.wikitext:
Bobby Vinton found the song in a reject pile at [[Epic Records]].<ref name=billboard/> He first recorded it as an [[R&B]] number, but was allowed to re-record it in a slower more dramatic arrangement, with strings and a vocal choir (from Robert Mersey and his Orchestra) added.<ref name="Levy"/><ref name=billboard/><ref name="ReferenceA">"Bobby Vinton's All-Time Greatest Hits," Varese (Vintage) Sarabande CD compilation, copyright 2003</ref>

The song was released in April 1962.<ref name="Levy">[[Alan Levy]], "[https://books.google.com/books?id=JkEEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA89 A dozen red roses - to disc jockeys]", ''[[Life (magazine)|Life]]'', March 12, 1965. p. 89</ref>  It reached No. 1 in Australia, New Zealand, Norway, South Africa, and the United States, and was a major hit in many other countries as well. The song topped the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] singles chart on July 14, 1962, and remained there for four weeks.<ref name="BillboardHot100">[https://www.billboard.com/artist/bobby-vinton/chart-history/hsi/ Hot 100 - Bobby Vinton Roses Are Red Chart History], ''Billboard.com''. Retrieved March 19, 2018.</ref><ref>[[Joel Whitburn]], "The Billboard Book of Top 40 Hits", ''Billboard Publications, Inc.'', 1987. p. 316</ref> The single was also the first number-one hit for [[Epic Records]].<ref name=billboard>{{cite book|last = Bronson|first = Fred|author-link = Fred Bronson|title = The Billboard Book of Number One Hits|publisher =Billboard Books|year = 2003| location = New York| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=PgGqNrqfrsoC&pg=PT122 |pages = 113|isbn = 9780823076772}}</ref>

''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' ranked the record No. 4 in their year end ranking "[[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1962|Top 100 Singles of 1962]]"<ref name="Top1001962">"[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/60s/1962/BB-1962-12-29-Who's-Who.pdf Top 100 Singles of 1962]", ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'', Section II, December 29, 1962. p. 82. Retrieved February 24, 2018.</ref> and No. 36 in their year end ranking of the top Rhythm and Blues records of 1962.<ref name="TopRB1962">"[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/60s/1962/BB-1962-12-29-Who's-Who.pdf The Top 50 Country Music and Rhythm & Blues Records of 1962]", ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'', Section II, December 29, 1962. p. 88. Retrieved March 19, 2018.</ref> The song was also ranked No. 17 on ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]''{{'}}s "Top 100 Chart Hits of 1962".<ref name="CBTop10062">{{cite magazine|title=Top 100 Chart Hits of 1962 |magazine=[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]|date=December 29, 1962 |page=10 |access-date= March 20, 2018|url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/60s/1962/CB-1962-12-29.pdf}}</ref>
sections.text:
Bobby Vinton found the song in a reject pile at Epic Records. He first recorded it as an R&B number, but was allowed to re-record it in a slower more dramatic arrangement, with strings and a vocal choir (from Robert Mersey and his Orchestra) added.

The song was released in April 1962.  It reached No. 1 in Australia, New Zealand, Norway, South Africa, and the United States, and was a major hit in many other countries as well. The song topped the Billboard Hot 100 singles chart on July 14, 1962, and remained there for four weeks. The single was also the first number-one hit for Epic Records.

Billboard ranked the record No. 4 in their year end ranking "Top 100 Singles of 1962" and No. 36 in their year end ranking of the top Rhythm and Blues records of 1962. The song was also ranked No. 17 on Cash Box{{'}}s "Top 100 Chart Hits of 1962".

sections.heading: Other versions
sections.wikitext:
In July 1962, [[David MacBeth]] released his version of the song as a single on [[Piccadilly Records]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.allmusic.com/artist/david-macbeth-mn0000178989|title=David MacBeth | Biography & History|website=[[AllMusic]]|access-date=6 May 2021}}</ref>

The song was recorded by [[Jim Reeves]] in 1963 and released on the album ''[[Gentleman Jim (album)|Gentleman Jim]]'', one of the last albums released while he was still alive.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.allmusic.com/album/gentleman-jim-mw0001144419 |title=Gentleman Jim - Jim Reeves |publisher= [[AllMusic]] |access-date=March 20, 2018}}</ref>

Caterina Valente recorded the song in German, ''Rosen Sind Rot''（1962). The single reached #7 in Germany.{{citation needed|date=April 2026}}

In 1962, an [[answer song]], entitled "Long as the Rose Is Red", was recorded by [[Florraine Darlin]].<ref>"[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/60s/1962/Billboard%201962-09-29.pdf Artists' Biographies]", ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'', September 29, 1962. p. 40. Accessed February 19, 2016</ref> The song spent seven weeks on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]], reaching No. 62,<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20180521230954/https://www.billboard.com/music/florraine-darlin/chart-history/hot-100/song/581650 Hot 100 - Florraine Darlin Long as the Rose Is Red Chart History], ''Billboard.com''. Retrieved March 20, 2018.</ref> while reaching No. 15 on ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]''{{'}}s [[Adult Contemporary (chart)|Easy Listening]] chart.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20180515090501/https://www.billboard.com/music/florraine-darlin/chart-history/adult-contemporary/song/581650 Adult Contemporary - Florraine Darlin Long as the Rose Is Red Chart History], ''Billboard.com''. Retrieved March 20, 2018.</ref><ref>"[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/60s/1962/Billboard%201962-09-15.pdf Easy Listening]", ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'', September 15, 1962. p. 26. Accessed February 19, 2016</ref> It was released by [[Epic Records]] (single #9529)<ref>"[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/60s/1962/Billboard%201962-08-04.pdf Late Pop Spotlights]", ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'', August 4, 1962. p. 10. Retrieved March 20, 2018.</ref> and was produced by Robert Morgan.
sections.text:
In July 1962, David MacBeth released his version of the song as a single on Piccadilly Records.

The song was recorded by Jim Reeves in 1963 and released on the album Gentleman Jim, one of the last albums released while he was still alive.

Caterina Valente recorded the song in German, Rosen Sind Rot（1962). The single reached #7 in Germany.{{citation needed|date=April 2026}}

In 1962, an answer song, entitled "Long as the Rose Is Red", was recorded by Florraine Darlin. The song spent seven weeks on the Billboard Hot 100, reaching No. 62, while reaching No. 15 on Billboard{{'}}s Easy Listening chart. It was released by Epic Records (single #9529) and was produced by Robert Morgan.
